name: Madison
title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Madison, WI | Genstone
metaDescription: Madison renovation contractor for investors: student rentals, isthmus duplexes, west side ranches, 203(k) and REO, with free pre-offer rehab reviews.
intro: Madison is a tight, high-demand housing market sitting on an isthmus between two lakes, and that combination changes how renovation math works. Purchase prices leave less room for error than in most Midwest cities, so a rehab here has to be precise: priced accurately before you buy, built to the standard the specific neighborhood rewards, and finished on a schedule that respects the city's unusual rental calendar. Genstone Construction manages renovations for investors, lenders and servicers in Madison and Dane County, coordinating vetted, licensed local contractors while our estimators and field managers run the project from our Romeoville, Illinois headquarters. Every engagement starts with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review that estimates repairs and checks your after-repair value against real local demand. You then receive a detailed scope with labor, materials and a draw schedule, a field manager assigned from start to finish, and no request for upfront payment. Dumpster and debris costs are built into every estimate.
housingStock:
Madison's housing falls into a few distinct bands, and each brings its own rehab profile.

The isthmus and the near east side, including Marquette, Tenney-Lapham and Schenk-Atwood, hold the city's oldest working-class housing: late nineteenth and early twentieth century frame houses, foursquares and Craftsman bungalows on narrow lots, many of them converted over the decades into two or three apartments. Expect balloon framing, plaster and lath, old wiring in the walls, stone or brick foundations and plenty of previous owner improvements of uneven quality.

Around the University of Wisconsin campus, Vilas, Greenbush and the Regent area mix early twentieth century single-family homes with houses chopped into student units. These buildings take heavy wear, and many carry layers of quick repairs from years of August turnovers.

The west side tells a different story. Dudgeon-Monroe has larger Tudor Revival and Colonial homes from the 1910s to the 1930s, while Westmorland and Midvale Heights shift to 1940s and 1950s Cape Cods and small ranches. Hill Farms, developed in the 1950s and 1960s, is known for mid-century ranches and split-levels.

On the east and north sides, Eken Park, Emerson East and Lake Edge are dominated by modest bungalows, post-war ranches and some 1960s and 1970s side-by-side duplexes. Farther out, subdivisions in the city and in Fitchburg, Sun Prairie and Verona are much newer.

For rehab budgets, the older bands mean lead-safe work, electrical upgrades and foundation moisture control; the mid-century bands bring asbestos in tile, siding and duct wrap, original electrical panels and aging sewer laterals.

One more pattern is worth knowing. Because Madison has been a tight market for a long time, many houses have been through several rounds of owner and landlord remodeling. That can work in your favor when a previous owner replaced the roof or furnace, but it also means finding finished basements without permits, attic bedrooms without egress and plumbing tied in with mismatched materials. A scope here should verify past work rather than assume it.

commonIssues.title: Wear from student and short-cycle tenancy
commonIssues.body: Houses near campus and on the isthmus often show the effects of years of student leasing: damaged doors and trim, patched drywall over plaster, worn floors, makeshift bedrooms and amateur electrical work. These properties can be excellent rentals, but a rehab should assume hidden repairs behind the cosmetic layer and plan for durable materials. Checking that every bedroom has legal egress and that the unit count matches what the city recognizes is part of our scope review.

commonIssues.title: Wet basements and high groundwater
commonIssues.body: Low-lying parts of the isthmus and areas near the Yahara River and the lakes are prone to high groundwater and seepage, and heavy rains in recent years have caused flooding in parts of the city. Older stone and block foundations let water in through joints and cracks. A sound Madison scope looks at grading, gutters, sump capacity and drain tile, and avoids finishing a lower level until water is under control.

commonIssues.title: Lead paint and older electrical
commonIssues.body: Houses built before 1978 make up much of the older rental stock in Madison, so lead-safe work practices apply on nearly every isthmus and east side job. These same houses commonly hide knob-and-tube wiring or ungrounded circuits behind plaster, along with overloaded panels added to by successive owners. Electrical updates are frequently a larger line item than investors expect, and they are best priced before purchase.

commonIssues.title: Asbestos in mid-century houses
commonIssues.body: West side and north side ranches and split-levels from the 1950s through the 1970s often contain asbestos in vinyl floor tile, mastic, textured ceilings, duct wrap and cement siding. These materials are usually safe when left intact, but disturbing them during a kitchen or flooring remodel requires proper testing and abatement. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review flags likely asbestos so it is priced into your plan rather than discovered mid-demolition.

commonIssues.title: Radon and lower-level conversions
commonIssues.body: Radon is a recognized concern across Wisconsin, and Dane County basements are no exception. Investors often want to finish a lower level to add a bedroom or family room, but that space should be tested and mitigated where needed. Egress windows, ceiling height and moisture also limit what a basement can legally become. We include radon testing and mitigation as a clear line item when lower-level space is part of the plan.

investorMarket:
Madison is not a deep-discount market, and investors who succeed here usually pick a strategy that matches the neighborhood.

Rental investors gravitate to the campus fringe and the isthmus, where student and young professional demand keeps units leased, and to east and north side neighborhoods like Emerson East, Eken Park and Sherman, where modest houses and duplexes serve working households. Demand for rentals in the city is strong, so the risk is less about vacancy and more about acquisition price and renovation cost.

Flipping works best on the near east and west sides, in places like Schenk-Atwood, Westmorland and Midvale Heights, where owner-occupant buyers compete for updated older homes. Margins are thinner than in cheaper markets, so the scope must be tight and the finish level must match recent sales, not exceed them.

BRRRR projects tend to happen on dated mid-century ranches, foreclosures and estate sales, where a buyer can add value through a full kitchen, bath and systems update and capture it at refinance.

Small multifamily remains one of the more sought-after assets in Madison. Converted houses on the isthmus and side-by-side duplexes on the south and east sides attract steady interest.

Surrounding communities such as Sun Prairie, Fitchburg and Monona offer newer stock where the rehab is lighter but competition from owner-occupants is significant.
permits:
Inside city limits, permits are issued by the City of Madison Building Inspection Division, which handles plan review and inspections for structural, electrical, plumbing and HVAC work. Remodels that add bedrooms, move walls, replace roofs, change the number of units or alter mechanical systems generally require permits, and trade work must be done by state-licensed electricians and plumbers. One- and two-family dwellings fall under Wisconsin's Uniform Dwelling Code, administered locally.

Two Madison-specific considerations come up often on investor jobs. First, the city has several local historic districts, including Mansion Hill, Third Lake Ridge, University Heights and the Marquette Bungalows district, where exterior changes such as windows, siding and porches may need review by the Madison Landmarks Commission. Second, changes to the number of units in a converted house can trigger zoning review, so confirming the legal unit count before purchase matters.

Suburbs such as Fitchburg, Middleton, Sun Prairie and Verona have their own building inspection offices and procedures. Genstone builds the correct jurisdiction's permits and inspections into the schedule for each property.
climate:
Madison winters are long and cold, and the lakes add humidity and occasional heavy snow, so ice dams form on houses with poor attic insulation and ventilation. Frost penetrates deeply, which is why porches, steps and slabs heave over time and need proper footings when rebuilt.

Spring melt and summer storms test drainage. Heavy rain events have flooded parts of the west side and areas along the Yahara River, so basement waterproofing and grading are part of many scopes.

For scheduling, exterior work such as roofing, siding, masonry and concrete is best handled from spring through fall. Interior renovations proceed year-round with heat maintained. Rental projects also follow the academic calendar, with many leases turning over in mid-August, so the summer months are the busiest and most important for rental turns near campus.

faqs.q: Is Madison a good market for fix-and-flip investors?
faqs.a: It can be, but the margins are usually narrower than in lower-priced Midwest cities. Demand from owner-occupants is strong, especially for updated older homes on the near east and west sides, yet acquisition prices are high. Successful Madison flips depend on accurate repair estimates and on choosing finishes that match recent sales. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review is designed to test those numbers before you commit.

faqs.q: Do you work on student rentals near the UW campus?
faqs.a: Yes. We renovate and turn rental properties in Vilas, Greenbush, the Regent area and the isthmus. Our scopes focus on durability, legal bedrooms with proper egress, safe electrical and fire protection. Because many leases in Madison turn over in August, we plan schedules around that window so units are ready when tenants arrive. Scoping in spring is the easiest way to secure contractor time before that late-summer rush begins.

faqs.q: Does Genstone have a local Madison office?
faqs.a: No. Madison projects are run out of our Romeoville, Illinois headquarters. For Madison projects, our estimators, field managers and billing team work from headquarters while we coordinate vetted, licensed and insured local contractors in Dane County. Your field manager oversees the job and shares progress, photos and milestones so you can follow along without visiting the site. That reporting is especially useful for investors who live outside Dane County.

faqs.q: What if my property is in a Madison historic district?
faqs.a: Exterior changes on properties in Madison's local historic districts may need approval from the Landmarks Commission, which can affect windows, siding, porches and additions. Interior work is generally not subject to that review. We identify whether a property is in a district during scoping and build any review time into the plan, choosing materials that are likely to be accepted.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Madison, WI | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Madison fix and flip renovations scoped against isthmus, east side and west side comps. Free pre-offer rehab review, finish options and work-based draws.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Madison
fix-flip.intro: Flipping in Madison is a precision exercise. Buyers are plentiful and well informed, many of them professionals tied to the university, state government or the region's health care and tech employers, but purchase prices are high enough that an overbuilt kitchen or an underestimated foundation repair can erase the profit. Genstone Construction scopes Madison flips against what has actually sold nearby. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates repairs, refines the after-repair value and tells you plainly whether the numbers support your offer. If they do, you get a detailed scope with labor, materials and a draw schedule, often with more than one finish plan, and a single field manager who runs the job through to listing. You pay nothing upfront, and draws are released as completed work is documented.

sections.body: Madison buyers segment sharply by neighborhood, and the right flip in Schenk-Atwood looks nothing like the right flip in Hill Farms. On the near east side, buyers want the character of an older house with modern systems: refinished wood floors, a kitchen that feels current without erasing the house's age, a restored front porch and a dry, usable basement. In Westmorland and Midvale Heights, Cape Cods and small ranches compete on a clean, open main floor, an updated bath, and sometimes a finished lower level. Hill Farms and similar mid-century neighborhoods attract buyers who appreciate original mid-century details, so a remodel that respects the design can outperform one that strips it out. Our estimators build finish plans to match these differences, and we will tell you when a higher finish level is not supported by the comps. That discipline is what protects margins in a market where purchase prices are already high and buyers have plenty of updated homes to compare against.

sections.h2: Systems and inspections on older Madison houses
sections.body: Madison buyers almost always order a home inspection, and older houses on the isthmus and east side tend to generate the same findings: knob-and-tube or ungrounded wiring, galvanized supply pipe, aging boilers, wet basements, and lead paint on windows and porches. Mid-century houses bring asbestos in flooring and duct wrap, original panels and tired sewer laterals. A flip that leaves these items unresolved invites renegotiation or a lost buyer. We address systems early in the scope, pull permits through the City of Madison Building Inspection Division, and keep documentation of what was replaced and when. Radon testing and mitigation are worth including on houses with finished or finishable lower levels, since many Dane County buyers ask about it. Presenting a full record of permits and updates at listing helps buyers and their lenders feel confident, which tends to shorten negotiations and keep the price closer to your target. It also helps when an appraiser needs to justify the value of an older house against newer homes.

sections.h2: Timing a Madison flip around seasons and the calendar
sections.body: Madison's housing market moves seasonally, with spring and early summer typically bringing the most buyer activity. A flip purchased in fall or early winter can use the cold months for interior work and be ready to list when spring demand returns, provided the exterior items are planned carefully. Roofing, siding, porch repairs and concrete are hard to complete in deep winter, so we either schedule them before the weather turns or plan them for early spring. Properties near campus have a different rhythm because investor and parent buyers watch the academic calendar, and a house with rental potential may sell well ahead of the August leasing season. Historic district properties may need Landmarks Commission review for exterior changes, which we build into the schedule. Your field manager posts progress and milestones so you can see whether the project is on track for your target listing date and adjust early if it is not.

faqs.q: How much should I spend on finishes for a Madison flip?
faqs.a: That depends entirely on the neighborhood and the comps. Buyers on the near east side and in parts of the west side pay for well-executed, character-preserving updates, while buyers of mid-century ranches focus on clean, functional spaces and updated systems. Our estimates often include more than one finish plan with costs and expected impact, so you can choose a level that matches recent sales instead of guessing.

faqs.q: Can you handle permits for a Madison flip?
faqs.a: Yes. We obtain the permits your scope requires from the City of Madison Building Inspection Division, or from the suburb's building office if the property sits outside city limits, and coordinate inspections as work progresses. If the house is in a local historic district, we identify any exterior work that needs Landmarks Commission review and plan for it in the schedule.

faqs.q: Do you offer financing for Madison flips?
faqs.a: Genstone Financial, part of the Genstone Companies, offers fix-and-flip loans, lines of credit, DSCR rental loans and new construction loans. Some investors pair our construction work with Genstone Financial to keep purchase and renovation under one group, while others bring their own lender. Either way, our scope and draw schedule give your lender the detail they need to release funds on time.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Madison, WI | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR rehabs in Madison and Dane County built to support the refinance appraisal and survive heavy rental use, from campus houses to east side ranches.
brrrr.intro: The BRRRR method works differently in Madison than in cheaper Midwest cities. Rental demand is strong and vacancy risk is relatively low, but entry prices are higher, which means the gap between purchase plus rehab and the refinance appraisal has to be engineered carefully. The opportunities usually come from dated houses that owner-occupant buyers pass over: estate sales on the west side, tired ranches on the north and east sides, and converted houses near campus that need a full systems update. Genstone Construction plans Madison BRRRR rehabs to hit that appraisal while building in the durability a long-term rental needs. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices the work and checks the after-repair value before you buy, and our detailed scope gives you a draw schedule that matches how rehab lenders release funds.

sections.h2: Where BRRRR math works in Madison
sections.body: The best Madison BRRRR candidates tend to share one trait: they look worse than they are. A 1950s ranch in Lake Edge or on the north side with original kitchen, original bath, carpet over hardwood and an old furnace can be bought below updated comps and brought up to their level with a disciplined scope. Estate-sale Cape Cods in Westmorland and Midvale Heights follow the same pattern, though competition for them can be sharper. Converted houses near campus can also work, but their value depends heavily on the legal unit and bedroom count, so we verify those details early. The houses that rarely work are those that need structural repairs or full foundation replacement, because the extra cost rarely shows up in an appraisal. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review walks through these factors and gives you a realistic cost and after-repair value range before you commit capital. In a market with strong competition from owner-occupants, that early clarity is what lets you bid with confidence.

Appraisers in Madison look for updated kitchens and baths, current mechanicals, sound roofs and windows, and dry, usable lower levels in the comparables they choose. A BRRRR scope should make the property clearly comparable to those updated homes. That typically means a full kitchen with durable cabinets and counters, a renovated bath, refinished hardwood or quality vinyl plank, fresh paint, updated lighting, and documented upgrades to heating, electrical and plumbing. If the house has a basement that can legally become a bedroom or family room, adding egress, managing moisture and mitigating radon may add value, but only where comps show finished lower levels. We pull permits through the City of Madison Building Inspection Division and keep the documentation the appraiser and refinance lender want to see. Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans if you want to line up long-term financing within the same group, though you can use any lender.

Madison renters include students, graduate students, hospital and university staff, and working families, and each group puts different stress on a property. Student-heavy units need hard-wearing floors, solid doors, simple fixtures and kitchens that can survive heavy use. Family rentals on the east and north sides benefit from durable finishes, a functional laundry and secure storage. Across all tenant types, the systems decisions matter most for long-term cash flow: replacing aging water heaters and furnaces during the rehab, upgrading electrical to handle modern loads, and solving basement moisture before tenants arrive. Lead-safe surfaces protect families and reduce later issues. We help you pick one rental-grade specification so future repairs are simple and inexpensive. Our one-year workmanship warranty covers the work we install, while tenant damage and normal wear fall outside it, which is why durable materials pay back over a long hold. Choosing them once, during the BRRRR rehab, keeps the property from needing a second capital round shortly after the refinance.

faqs.q: Can a BRRRR deal work in Madison's high-priced market?
faqs.a: Yes, but it requires careful selection. Properties that look dated but are structurally sound, such as mid-century ranches and estate-sale homes, offer the best spread between purchase price plus rehab and the post-renovation appraisal. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review tests that spread before you buy, so you are not relying on optimistic assumptions in a market where purchase prices are already strong.

faqs.q: What records help a Madison BRRRR appraisal?
faqs.a: Your field manager records each stage with photos, notes and milestones, and we keep permits and inspection records on file. At the end of the project you can share a clear list of what was replaced and updated, from mechanicals to finishes. That record helps the appraiser understand the scope and supports your refinance lender's review, especially on older houses.

faqs.q: Should I finish the basement on a Madison BRRRR?
faqs.a: Only if the comps support it and the space can legally be used. Finished lower levels need dry conditions, adequate ceiling height, egress for any bedroom and, ideally, radon testing and mitigation. If neighboring updated homes have finished basements, adding one may lift the appraisal. If they do not, the money is often better spent on the kitchen, bath and systems.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Madison, WI | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Rental renovations in Madison for campus houses, isthmus conversions and east side homes, with durable specs and turns timed to the August lease cycle.
rental-renovation.intro: Owning rentals in Madison means working around a calendar most cities do not have. A large share of leases near the University of Wisconsin turn over in mid-August, and the weeks around that date compress cleaning, painting, repairs and move-ins into a narrow window that every landlord and contractor in town is competing for. Away from campus, east and north side rentals serve working families and professionals who stay longer but expect well-kept homes. Genstone Construction renovates Madison single-family homes, converted houses and duplexes for owners who want reliable tenant-ready units. We write a portfolio specification, plan renovations months ahead of turnover, and assign a field manager who coordinates vetted local contractors and keeps documentation visible to you and your property manager.

sections.body: Owners with campus-area rentals know that summer is the only realistic time for major renovations, and that the final weeks before the mid-August move-in are the most crowded. The better plan is to scope early. We prefer to walk properties in late winter or spring, finalize scopes and materials before units empty, and start work as soon as tenants leave. Larger tasks such as kitchen replacements, flooring, bathroom remodels and electrical upgrades go first, while paint, cleaning and final touches fill the last stretch before move-in. If a unit becomes vacant outside the usual cycle, we use that opportunity for work that is hard to fit into summer. Your field manager tracks every unit against the move-in date and flags any risk early, so you are not discovering in August that a bathroom will not be finished. That planning is often the difference between a full lease-up and a month of lost rent.

sections.h2: A durable spec for Madison rental housing
sections.body: A rental specification that works in Madison has to hold up to student wear near campus and to longer family tenancies elsewhere. Luxury vinyl plank in kitchens, baths and common areas resists water and scuffs. Solid-core doors and sturdy hardware survive frequent move-ins. Simple, widely stocked fixtures make repairs easy. Kitchens benefit from durable counters and cabinet boxes that resist moisture. For safety and compliance, every bedroom needs proper egress, smoke and carbon monoxide detection must be current, and electrical systems should be free of overloaded or unsafe circuits, which are common in older converted houses on the isthmus. Lead-safe work practices apply on pre-1978 homes. We write these choices into a standard spec that applies across your portfolio, so a renovated unit on Spaight Street and one in Eken Park share fixtures, colors and materials, simplifying maintenance and future turns. It also speeds up scoping for each new acquisition, because our estimators can price against a known standard.

The expenses that hurt Madison rental owners over time are usually hidden ones: basement seepage during spring melt or heavy summer storms, frozen pipes in an older house during a deep cold snap, and failing water heaters or boilers. Renovation is the right time to address them. We look at grading, gutters, sump pumps and foundation repair when water is entering, add attic insulation and air sealing where ice dams have formed, and replace aging mechanical equipment before it fails mid-lease. On mid-century homes, asbestos in flooring or duct wrap is handled properly when work disturbs it. Between full renovations, Genstone Field Services can handle turn and make-ready work, inspections and occupied maintenance, giving you one coordinated team across the full rental cycle. Our one-year workmanship warranty covers our installation work, though tenant damage and normal wear are not included. Fixing the root causes during a renovation keeps those uncovered costs low.

faqs.q: Can you turn many Madison units before the August move-in?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as planning starts early. We recommend scoping units in spring, ordering materials ahead of time and scheduling work from the day tenants move out. Because the late-summer window is crowded, early commitment matters. Your field manager tracks each unit against its move-in date and keeps you updated if anything threatens the schedule, so you can adjust move-in plans in time.

faqs.q: Do you renovate rentals outside the campus area?
faqs.a: Yes. Many of our Madison rental projects are on the east and north sides, in neighborhoods like Emerson East, Eken Park and Lake Edge, as well as in nearby communities such as Fitchburg and Sun Prairie. These rentals often need systems updates and durable finishes more than heavy cosmetic work, and the scheduling is more flexible than campus-area turns throughout the year.

faqs.q: How do you keep finishes consistent across properties?
faqs.a: We create a rental specification with you that lists flooring, paint, fixtures, cabinets, counters and hardware. Every renovation in your portfolio follows that spec unless you choose otherwise. That consistency makes repairs faster and cheaper, helps your property manager keep supplies on hand and gives tenants a predictable standard across your buildings. You can update the spec at any time as products change.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex & 2–4 Unit Renovation in Madison, WI | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Madison duplex and 2–4 unit renovations: isthmus house conversions, side-by-side duplexes and small apartment buildings, phased around occupied units.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Duplex and 2–4 Unit Renovations in Madison
multifamily-renovation.intro: Madison's small multifamily stock comes in two main forms. On the isthmus and near campus, many older houses were divided long ago into two, three or four apartments, sometimes with creative layouts, shared stairways and systems that grew one tenant at a time. On the south, east and west sides, purpose-built side-by-side duplexes from the 1960s and 1970s offer simpler, more uniform layouts. Both are sought after, and both need renovation scopes that respect legal unit counts, fire separation and shared systems. Genstone Construction renovates Madison duplexes and small multifamily properties for investors and owners, often while some units remain occupied. Every project starts with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review and a detailed scope, and one field manager handles the building from start to finish.

sections.h2: Converted houses on the isthmus and near campus
sections.body: Converted houses in Marquette, Tenney-Lapham, Vilas and the campus fringe can be excellent assets, but they often carry decades of piecemeal changes. Stairways may have been enclosed or added, attics turned into bedrooms, and utilities split in ways that make sense only to past owners. Before renovating, we verify the legal unit count and bedroom configuration, since adding or reconfiguring units in Madison may require zoning approval. The scope then focuses on safety and durability: fire separation between units, proper egress from every bedroom including attic spaces, updated electrical service sized for multiple households, separate or clearly allocated heating, and plumbing stacks that can handle multiple kitchens and baths. Properties within local historic districts may need Landmarks Commission review for exterior work, so window or porch replacements are planned with that in mind. The result is a building that leases more easily and generates far fewer emergency calls from its tenants.

sections.h2: Side-by-side duplexes on the south, east and west sides
sections.body: Side-by-side duplexes are common across Madison's mid-century neighborhoods, including parts of the south and west sides and the areas around Lake Edge and Monona. These buildings tend to have mirrored layouts, separate entrances and often separate utilities, which makes them easier to manage than converted houses. Their renovation needs are predictable: dated kitchens and baths, original windows, worn flooring, older furnaces and water heaters, and sometimes asbestos in flooring, siding or duct wrap. The party wall and the shared roof structure deserve attention, especially when one side has been well maintained and the other has not. We typically renovate both units to the same specification so rents and appraisals stay aligned, and we schedule exterior work, roofing and siding as a single project for the whole building. Keeping the two halves consistent also makes resale simpler, since buyers evaluate the duplex as one income property and quickly notice any mismatch between sides.

Many small multifamily buildings in Madison are purchased with tenants in place, and with the city's strong rental demand, vacancy is rarely something an owner wants to create. Phasing lets you renovate without displacing residents. A common approach is to renovate each unit fully when it turns over, while scheduling shared-system work, such as electrical service upgrades, heating replacement, roofing and basement waterproofing, with advance notice and short, planned interruptions. On campus-area buildings, the August turnover is often the best opportunity to renovate several units at once. Throughout, we follow lead-safe practices on older buildings and keep common areas clean and safe each day. Your field manager coordinates access with tenants and your property manager, and posts progress so you can see each unit's status and how it fits the overall building plan. That transparency helps you set realistic lease dates for newly renovated units and avoid overlapping move-ins across the building.

faqs.q: Can I add a unit to a Madison house during renovation?
faqs.a: Possibly, but it depends on zoning, the lot and the building. Adding a dwelling unit usually requires zoning review and permits, and it brings fire separation, egress and utility requirements. We can help you assess whether a conversion is realistic and price the work, but the approval process with the city needs to be confirmed before you commit. We will not assume an approval that has not been granted.

faqs.q: Do Madison duplexes need separate utilities?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, but separate heating and electrical services make tenant billing simpler and often improve net income. Many side-by-side duplexes already have them, while converted houses often share systems. We can price separation as a distinct line item, letting you compare the cost against your expected hold period and rental income. Where gas and electric work is involved, utility coordination is planned into the schedule from the start.

faqs.q: How do you handle a building where some units are occupied?
faqs.a: We phase the work. Vacant units are renovated first, shared systems are updated with planned notice and short interruptions, and occupied units are renovated when tenants move out. Your field manager coordinates with residents and your property manager to keep the building safe, clean and livable throughout the process. Lead-safe containment is used wherever painted surfaces in older buildings are disturbed.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Madison, WI | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor for Madison buyers, agents and lenders: bids, consultant reports and draws for east side bungalows and older homes.
fha-203k.intro: In a competitive market like Madison, many first-time buyers find that the houses within their budget are the ones nobody else wants: an east side bungalow with an original kitchen and a wet basement, a north side ranch with an aging furnace and asbestos tile, or a duplex that needs both units refreshed. The FHA 203(k) loan lets a buyer finance the purchase and the repairs together, turning those overlooked houses into realistic options. Genstone Construction is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor working with Madison buyers, real estate agents and loan officers. We prepare bids and scopes in the format lenders need, coordinate with HUD consultants, and manage the renovation through the draw process so the buyer ends up with the house the loan was meant to deliver.

sections.h2: Choosing between Standard and Limited in Madison
sections.body: Genstone follows the FHA 203(k) thresholds as stated on our site: the minimum repair amount is $5,000, a HUD consultant inspection is involved above $15,000, and the Limited 203(k) caps repairs at $75,000 and does not allow structural work. In Madison, a Limited 203(k) often fits a 1950s ranch or Cape Cod that needs a new furnace, updated electrical, new flooring and a kitchen refresh. A Standard 203(k) is the better fit when the house needs foundation repair, structural changes, major waterproofing or a full gut of an older isthmus home. The choice matters because switching programs midway can delay closing. Our estimators look for structural red flags, such as bowing basement walls, sagging floors or damaged framing, early in the process so the buyer and loan officer can choose the right program from the start. Isthmus houses with stone foundations and older framing deserve particular scrutiny, while many mid-century houses on the west and north sides fit comfortably within a Limited scope.

Madison 203(k) projects often combine required health and safety work with improvements the buyer wants. Required items commonly include peeling paint on pre-1978 houses, which calls for lead-safe work, unsafe or outdated electrical, failing roofs, aging heating systems, missing handrails and moisture problems in basements. Asbestos in mid-century flooring and duct wrap may need to be addressed if it will be disturbed. Radon testing and mitigation are often worth including given the regional concern. Optional improvements tend to focus on kitchens, bathrooms, refinished floors and energy efficiency, such as attic insulation, air sealing and new windows suited to Wisconsin winters. We separate required and optional items clearly in the bid, so the buyer and lender can see what must be completed and what can be adjusted if the appraisal or budget is tight. That clarity reduces surprises at underwriting and keeps the closing timeline realistic for everyone involved, including the listing agent.

For a Standard 203(k), the HUD consultant writes the work write-up and our bid aligns with it item by item. We review the consultant's report, flag anything that may cost more once walls or floors are opened, and keep revisions to a minimum so the lender is not waiting. After closing, our field manager pulls the permits the work requires from the City of Madison Building Inspection Division, or from the suburb's building department if the house is outside city limits, and coordinates required inspections. Renovation funds are released in draws as work is completed and inspected, and we provide photos and documentation for each stage. Agents benefit because the renovation side of the transaction is organized and predictable. Buyers benefit from a single field manager who explains what is happening and when they can move in. Exterior items that cannot be finished during a Madison winter are scheduled for spring with the lender's agreement.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) loan be used on a Madison duplex?
faqs.a: Yes. FHA allows 203(k) financing on properties with one to four units, provided the buyer occupies one unit as a primary residence. This makes the program a practical path to owning a Madison duplex or converted house. Your loan officer confirms eligibility, and we can prepare a scope that covers each unit and the shared systems, including heat and the roof.

faqs.q: How early should a Madison buyer contact Genstone?
faqs.a: As early as possible, ideally while the buyer and agent are evaluating the property. An early walkthrough or preliminary estimate helps everyone understand whether the house fits a Limited or Standard 203(k) and whether the numbers work. Once the offer is accepted, we finalize the bid to match the consultant's report and the lender's requirements without delay, keeping the closing date intact.

faqs.q: Does the buyer pay Genstone before work starts?
faqs.a: No. Renovation funds in a 203(k) loan are held by the lender and released in draws after completed work is inspected. Genstone asks for nothing upfront from the buyer. Final payment comes after completion and approval, and our field manager provides the documentation each draw requires. That structure protects the buyer, because money moves only when the work has actually been done and inspected.

reo-renovation.title: REO Property Renovation in Madison, WI | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: Bank-owned and REO renovations in Madison and Dane County for servicers, banks, GSEs and investors: securing, moisture, mold, code work and resale repairs.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Renovations in Madison
reo-renovation.intro: REO inventory in Madison is thinner than in many Midwest cities because demand absorbs homes quickly, but the bank-owned and vacant properties that do appear often need careful handling. A vacant isthmus house or west side ranch may have sat through a winter without heat, taken on basement water during a storm or developed mold behind finished walls. In a market where buyers are plentiful, the condition of the property largely determines how fast and at what price it sells. Genstone Construction works with mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and investors purchasing REO in Madison, and we are a preferred contractor for Government-Sponsored Enterprises. Together with Genstone Field Services, we can secure, document, repair and prepare a property for market.

sections.body: The first visit to a vacant Madison property focuses on what has happened since the owner left. Heat may have been shut off, leading to frozen supply lines and cracked fixtures. Sump pumps may have failed during spring melt or summer storms, leaving basements wet and encouraging mold growth. Roof leaks may have gone unnoticed in an attic that nobody checked. We document every condition with photos and notes, pressure-test plumbing, check heating systems and look for moisture in lower levels. That information goes to the asset manager along with a scope that separates urgent items, such as winterization, securing doors and windows, stopping water intrusion and mold remediation, from the repairs needed for sale. Quick, clear documentation helps servicers approve emergency work without delay. It also helps them plan the rest of the repairs with full knowledge of the property's condition and its likely resale position in this neighborhood.

Madison neighborhoods tend to be closely watched, and vacant properties that look neglected draw complaints and inspections quickly. Overgrown yards, unshoveled walks, broken windows and accumulated debris can all lead to orders from the city. Genstone Field Services handles property preservation, including lawn care, snow removal, debris removal, lock changes and routine inspections, along with code compliance work. When open orders exist, we review them, price the needed repairs, obtain permits from the City of Madison Building Inspection Division and coordinate reinspection. Properties within local historic districts require extra care, since exterior repairs such as window replacement may need Landmarks Commission review. Keeping a vacant property in good order protects its value and maintains good relations with neighbors, which can matter when the house is eventually listed and buyers walk the block. In winter, prompt snow removal and regular checks of heat and plumbing are the most important preservation tasks.

Because Madison has strong buyer demand, many REO properties can sell well with targeted repairs rather than full renovations. The right scope depends on the neighborhood and the likely buyer. An older house on the near east side may attract owner-occupants who want move-in condition and will pay for refinished floors and an updated kitchen. A mid-century ranch on the north side may sell to investors who prefer a lower price and plan their own updates. FHA and conventional buyers need a property that meets lender standards, which usually means working mechanical systems, safe electrical, a sound roof and no active water intrusion. Our estimators prepare scope options with detailed costs so asset managers can compare strategies. Throughout the work, we provide documentation, permits, lien waivers and milestone updates, with a single field manager responsible from start to finish. Timing the listing for spring, when Madison buyer activity is usually strongest, is often worth planning around.

faqs.q: Who does Genstone serve on Madison REO projects?
faqs.a: We work with mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and individual investors purchasing bank-owned properties, and we are a preferred contractor for Government-Sponsored Enterprises. Each client receives a detailed scope, photo documentation and a field manager who stays with the property from the first visit through completion. Genstone Field Services can handle preservation while the asset awaits a repair decision.

faqs.q: How do you handle mold in a vacant Madison house?
faqs.a: We identify and document affected areas, address the moisture source, remove damaged materials and include remediation as a separate scope item. In Madison, moisture problems often come from failed sump pumps, groundwater during heavy rains or frozen pipes, so solving the source is part of the plan to prevent recurrence after the property is sold. Photos document conditions before and after.

faqs.q: Can Genstone maintain a vacant property before repairs start?
faqs.a: Yes. Our sister company, Genstone Field Services, covers preservation, inspections, code compliance and related upkeep for vacant homes. For vacant Madison properties, that can include lawn care, snow removal, securing the home and regular inspections, which help protect the asset and limit neighbor complaints while decisions are made. Inspection reports with photos are shared with the asset manager after each visit.
